rationale: Six independent instances in six domains. In search-agent training, removing the terminal outcome reward costs 6.3 F1 - larger than removing either dense per-step signal - and is the only ablation that degrades every benchmark; the process weight sweep peaks at 0.25 and collapses to 44.8 at 1.00, below several baselines. In multi-domain translation, removing the sequence-level quality reward is likewise the largest degradation (in-domain BLEU 29.83 to 22.94), well ahead of removing the process reward or its token-level distribution. In audio reasoning, accuracy declines past a rubric weight of 0.5 because the policy optimizes for satisfying criteria rather than for being right, and a length penalty had to be added because more criteria are satisfied by longer traces. A fourth design makes the constraint explicit rather than empirical: bounding a privileged-teacher correction by the magnitude of the outcome advantage means it can never flip a sign or create an update where the outcome reward is silent. Two further instances added on 2026-08-20 also show how the failure looks from the outside, which the earlier four did not. In video-anomaly tool orchestration, removing the task-completion reward drops whole-response accuracy from 95.14% to 29.92% - by far the largest ablation, and larger than removing the LLM-judge process terms entirely, which costs 1.44 points - while decision accuracy and tool-selection accuracy both remain at a perfect 100%: the agent chooses correctly at every step and never stops. In subjective verification, a length incentive that is not gated on the answer being correct is satisfied vacuously rather than ignored: an unconstrained length reward is exploited to the 8192-token context limit with macro-F1 falling to 0.210, and a bounded target-constrained penalty buys about 990 tokens of coherent but functionally useless filler at 0.760, essentially the collapsed level, while the same reward gated on correctness reaches 0.851. Together these sharpen the mechanism: a process signal decoupled from the outcome is not merely weak, it is satisfiable without being used, and per-step metrics can saturate while the trajectory as a whole is worthless. The practical reading is that a process signal refines the distribution of credit along a trajectory and cannot supply its direction. A seventh source, added 2026-08-20, converts the constraint from an empirical regularity into a design pattern. Training a long-horizon tool-using video agent, it applies turn-level credit as a multiplicative modulation of the trajectory-level advantage -- preserving that advantage's sign and direction while reweighting only its magnitude -- and states the reason in exactly these terms: additive turn rewards introduce competing local signals that can conflict with the final-answer reward and misassign credit, especially over long horizons, whereas multiplication yields direction-consistent credit refinement. The additive variant of their own method is 1.6 and 2.0 points worse on two benchmarks, and its training curves are less stable. So the rule generalises beyond weighting: a process signal should gate or modulate an outcome signal rather than be added to it, because addition lets a local term outvote the terminal one while gating and modulation cannot. The same paper supplies a second instance of the principle in its training-regime ablation, where a policy trained by reinforcement learning alone cannot invoke its tools at all -- 50.6 percent format compliance against 100 for the full pipeline -- so the imitation stage is a precondition for the outcome signal to have anything well-formed to select among.
statement: Dense process reward works only as a modifier on an outcome signal, never as a replacement: across every paper measuring it, removing the terminal reward is the largest single ablation loss, and pushing the process weight too high drives performance below the baseline it was meant to improve.
